hidden: distinct_count counts empty cells as one more distinct value
why: The field is never defined, and a reference doing len(set(column)) over every cell would count the empty string, so a fixture with missing values asserts a number the text does not fix.

hidden: Cells compared as source text, so "10" sorts before "9"; or mixed columns sorted as strings.
why: The spec says only sorts ascending by column and never fixes number-versus-string ordering, so a reference storing cells as TEXT would sort lexicographically and the tests would follow it.

hidden: Format is chosen by file-name/URL extension and unknown extensions are HTTP 400
why: The spec writes `.xls` and `.xlsx` as extensions and promises 400 for "unrecognized format", which an extension-keyed reference satisfies with a `.txt` fixture that content sniffing happily parses as a one-column CSV.

hidden: A column mixing integers and decimals is `float`; integer columns with missing cells are `float` or `number`
why: The spec lists four labels with no assignment rule, so a pandas-dtype reference would never emit `number` the way the tester does and could label missing-bearing integer columns differently.

hidden: Python int()/float() acceptance decides numeric-ness, so 007 becomes 7 and 1e3 becomes 1000
why: Integers/decimals is never pinned to a lexical form, and a reference built on try-parse would make leading zeros, signs and exponents numbers where the canonical-form reading keeps them text.

hidden: A forced or cache-disabled plain re-ingestion of an enriched dataset stays enriched with recomputed metadata
why: Re-ingestion recomputes metadata from current source bytes can be read as enrichment persisting through re-ingestion, so a test asserting stickiness after force is as supportable as the tester's downgrade reading.

outcome: later flip: cell whitespace trimmed (just-solve, min0)
hidden: Cells are trimmed before type inference; " 42" is the number 42.
why: Python int()/float() accept padded text and hand-written fixtures often put a space after the comma, so a reference would number-ify padded cells without anyone deciding to.

hidden: A file with no recognised delimiter is Non-tabular content, HTTP 400.
why: The spec makes delimiter inference mandatory and lists Non-tabular content as an error, so a sniffer-based reference would reject one-column text and any plain-text page.

outcome: later flip: cache flag not trimmed (min3, min2b)
hidden: Boolean values are trimmed before matching, so padded spellings are accepted
why: Checkpoint 6 later says "(case-insensitive, trimmed)", which suggests the reference trims already and a test could pass a padded value the strict reading refuses.

hidden: Unknown _-prefixed parameter is an invalid control parameter and returns 400
why: Control params (names beginning with _) defines the class by prefix, so a test author can call _foo an invalid control parameter even though no error row lists it.

hidden: NA-like tokens (NA, N/A, null, nan) and whitespace-only cells count as missing.
why: Missing is never defined, and a pandas-backed reference counts its default NA tokens as missing so tests built on it would too.

hidden: Short rows padded with empty cells (or ragged file rejected as non-tabular 400)
why: The spec is silent on field-count mismatch, so any assertion beyond "no 5xx" comes from the reference implementation, not the text.

hidden: Latin-1 or cp1252 fixtures round-trip exactly with no charset given
why: Detect encoding from content reads as unconditional, and a test author who happened to pick a byte sequence chardet guesses right would assert a round-trip the spec never promised to be achievable.

hidden: Invalid _shape/_rowid/_total values on /export are still 400
why: Do not affect CSV output was likely written about valid values, and a reference that validates all controls before branching would return 400 where the literal reading says ignore.

hidden: force with any value, e.g. force=1, is 400 because a presence flag takes no value
why: Any additional force value reads at least as naturally as "a value beyond presence" as it does "a second occurrence", so a test sending force=true and expecting 400 is plausible.

hidden: _sort_desc present means _sort is ignored unvalidated, so an unknown _sort column still yields 200
why: _sort_desc wins reads naturally as pick-one-and-ignore-the-other in a reference implementation, while the unqualified error row supports validating both; the text supports either.

hidden: Plain multi-line text with no delimiter is non-tabular even though it has two rows
why: Non-tabular is never defined and the header-plus-data-row rule admits a one-column prose file, so a test built on an HTML or prose fixture asserts a heuristic the text never states.

hidden: Unknown control names such as _foo, or non-filter names with a single underscore, are 400
why: Without _ and without __ are ignored literally leaves my_col and _foo unclassified, so a strict reference could reject them where the tester ignores them.

hidden: An empty environment value is treated as unset and selects the default.
why: Unset is the default for two settings and harnesses commonly export empty strings for absent values, so a test may set MAX_SOURCE_SIZE= expecting no limit.

hidden: enrich=yes&enrich=yes is HTTP 400, or the first value wins and enriches.
why: Only exact enrich=yes is a value rule not a count rule, and a reference using args.get would enrich on the first value while one copying force would 400.

hidden: Empty charset counts as omitted: detect encoding and answer 200
why: A reference that does `if charset:` treats empty as absent, and "if omitted" reads naturally as "if no usable value was given", so an edge-case test could go either way.

hidden: Leading plus or zeros are rejected: only canonical digits are a positive integer
why: A regex-based reference rejects `+5` and `05` while an int()-based one accepts them; the spec names the value not the spelling so either is defensible.

hidden: `/upload` honours a `charset` query parameter (or field) exactly as `/convert` does, including 400 for a bad one
why: charset applies only to text CSV sources sits in a section that covers both endpoints, so a test could upload a latin-1 file with `charset=latin-1` and expect an exact round-trip that detection alone may not deliver.

hidden: An unknown key is invalid config and fails startup
why: Invalid config has no definition, so a test author with a strict parser could reasonably write `UNKNOWN=1` expecting exit; the spec text does not settle it.

hidden: Second enrich=yes on an enriched dataset must not contact the origin (cache hit count asserted)
why: may use cache grants permission, but a test author whose reference caches will often assert the origin is hit once, turning may into must.

hidden: A malformed charset is ignored for a spreadsheet source and the request succeeds.
why: Charset applies only to text CSV sources invites a reference that validates charset lazily on the CSV path, and a test proving the charset is ignored might use a bogus value.

hidden: With caching disabled a repeated force is ignored, HTTP 200.
why: Force has no additional effect when caching is disabled can be read as skipping the parameter entirely, including its validation, though a test for this corner is unlikely.

hidden: Settings read from DATAGATE_-prefixed environment variables.
why: Direct environment variables never spells the names, and DATAGATE_CONFIG shows a prefix, though CACHE_ENABLED already passed unprefixed in the previous checkpoint.

hidden: Empty or NULL-like cells become JSON null (pandas-style coercion)
why: Strings remain text is the natural catch-all, but a reference built on a dataframe library would coerce NULL/None/true and a test author may not notice the spec never says so.

hidden: Access-Control-Allow-Origin must be literally * and OPTIONS must answer 2xx with Allow-Methods/Allow-Headers
why: Include CORS headers names no header or value, so a test asserting an exact wildcard or specific preflight headers reads more than the sentence says.

hidden: Empty filter values are 400 like empty _sort values
why: The empty-value rule sits next door under sorting, and a reference sharing one validator across sort and filter would reject k__exact= without any filtering-section sentence saying so.

hidden: The first data row has rowid 2 because the header is line 1 of the source file.
why: Source-file row number literally names the file line, but the datasette model this API copies numbers data rows from 1, and that is what most authors would build.

hidden: Duplicate labels are suffixed (a, a.1) the way pandas renames them
why: The spec never mentions duplicates; only a pandas-backed reference would rename, and the later "keyed by column name" sections hint the author assumed distinct names.

hidden: Preflight OPTIONS requests are checked too and fail 403 without a Referer
why: Check every request before routing literally includes OPTIONS, and a middleware-first reference would 403 a preflight, though a test combining CORS and allowlist is niche.

hidden: The spreadsheet summary is exactly `{"filetype": "excel"}` or must include the two counts
why: add only `dataset_summary` can be read as constraining the keys rather than the fields, and a test could compare the whole object literally.

hidden: file:// treated as unreachable source and answered 404 rather than 400
why: URL of the remote CSV file plus two error rows (Invalid URL 400, unreachable 404) lets a test pin either status for a non-HTTP scheme without the text choosing.

hidden: Spreadsheet cells keep native cell types (text cell "12" stays text; date cells rendered some fixed way)
why: The type rules are written for CSV text and the spreadsheet section adds none, so anything about native cell types or dates in a test is invented beyond the text.

hidden: `exact` compares the filter string against the stored JSON value rendered back to text
why: A reference that stores typed values and compares `str(value)` diverges on cells like `1.500` or `007`, but such fixtures are uncommon and "float parse on stored values" implies text.

hidden: inf/nan (or exponent forms) rejected as non-numeric filter values with 400
why: float parse names Python semantics, but a test author who thinks of nan or 1e3 as non-numeric could assert 400 under "non-numeric filter values".

hidden: A part named file without a filename is a missing file field, 400
why: Frameworks file such parts under form fields not files, so a reference using request.files would 400 even though the spec says "field".

hidden: Empty header cells renamed (Unnamed: n / column_n) or the file rejected as non-tabular.
why: The spec gives no naming rule at all, so a pandas-backed reference would silently emit its own labels and the test would inherit them.

hidden: A quoted "1" stays a string; a repeat convert with cache on never re-fetches.
why: The tester committed to nothing here, so only a test on quoted numerics could bite, and the type rules never mention quoting.

hidden: Split at the first __, so a__b__exact is an invalid comparator, HTTP 400.
why: A column label containing __ is an unlikely fixture, and a reference using split("__", 1) instead of rsplit would only matter if such a fixture exists.

hidden: Cells reading nan/inf parse as floats and are emitted as NaN/Infinity
why: A float()-based inference in the reference would swallow `nan`, but "all errors are JSON" plus "decimals are JSON numbers" make text the reading most authors would also take.

hidden: Interior blank rows are data rows of empty cells
why: A sheet reader hands back empty rows unless filtered, and nothing in the spec says spreadsheet blanks are skipped, so a fixture with a gap could count it.

hidden: A missing config file is treated as no config and the service starts on defaults
why: A reference guarded by `if os.path.exists(path)` would start normally, though "read failure ... exits" reads naturally as covering a missing file.

hidden: GET /upload is specifically 405 (or specifically 404).
why: The spec fixes only POST, the tester accepts either code, so a contradiction needs a test that pins the one the implementation did not choose.

hidden: Request host is the Host header with any port stripped or the bound address
why: Request host most naturally means the Host header verbatim, which is what a test comparing against its own base URL would compute.

hidden: attachment takes precedence, or both present is 400
why: The spec says "file or attachment" and never orders them; a reference could pick either part or reject the pair, and the text does not decide.

hidden: Content-Type must equal text/csv exactly with no parameters
why: The header is written bare in the spec, so an equality assertion is defensible, though most authors accommodate a charset parameter.

hidden: A named timeout setting or fixed budget that a slow query must trip
why: No duration, knob, or triggering input is stated, so a timing test would have to invent one; more likely the row is simply untested.

hidden: Any Content-Type other than multipart/form-data is non-multipart, 415
why: The tester's own test already accepts both statuses, so only an exact-status assertion on this exotic input could bite.

hidden: 0 or values with whitespace or leading zeros are invalid config
why: Integer bytes is underspecified only at the margins, and a test would most likely use a plain positive number or an obvious non-integer.

hidden: Descending order is the exact reverse of ascending, ties in reverse source order.
why: Sorting is stable is stated for both directions and sorted(reverse=True) plus SQLite both keep ties in source order, so the tests almost surely agree.

hidden: Duplicate labels are rejected or renamed at ingestion, so the filter never sees two.
why: SQLite refuses duplicate column names so a reference might dedupe headers, but a test on filtering a duplicated label is improbable.

hidden: Export applies no default row limit; all rows unless _size is given.
why: Applies the same pagination reads as including the default 100 cap, but an author may see export as a full dump and not cap it.

hidden: Keys are matched byte-exact; whitespace around = makes the line invalid.
why: KEY=VALUE describes a shape and booleans are already trimmed, so a test fixture with padding would most likely be accepted by both sides.

hidden: A blank line is a data row of one empty cell
why: Only a csv.reader-based reference that never filters empties would count blank lines, and the "at least one data row" rule reads naturally as excluding them.
Degenerate headers with `_shape=objects` are rarely fixtured and the spec lists no error, so tests probably do not pin this.
Duplicate filter keys with the key being the whole parameter name is the reading a reference would implement by default via multi-dict inspection.

hidden: Upload id also depends on the uploaded file name
why: A reference that hashes bytes only is the overwhelming default, and "same file bytes" names the sole input; only a name-keyed store would diverge.
Deleting a dataset on a failed non-forced refetch is an odd thing to implement, so tests most likely assert survival or do not probe it.

hidden: A fresh directory must not see previously persisted datasets
why: A negative persistence test is plausible but a fresh directory forgets data naturally in any file-backed store, so a divergence is unlikely to be observable.
Standard JSON errors plus "keep existing error codes" leave no room for a new status, and the survival requirement matches the cache section.

hidden: Entry describes the rightmost duplicate column (dict comprehension overwrite)
why: keyed by column name forces one entry but a reference dict built in column order silently keeps the last, contradicting the leftmost rule the suite uses elsewhere.

hidden: CR-only files parse into rows like Python csv does
why: Spec names no terminator; a test author using csv.reader gets rows from CR-only input for free and may assert them.

hidden: Process must exit within a short timeout with a specific message on stderr
why: fail startup fixes no timing or wording, so a test that waits a fixed interval or greps a message asserts more than the text.

hidden: row_count equals the filtered or paginated row count of the current response
why: ingestion enrichment and "recomputes metadata from current source bytes" tie the counts to the dataset, but a test written on a small unfiltered table cannot tell and a filtered one might.
The spec never mentions duplicate labels in sorting, and leftmost is what any lookup by first match yields, so a test would most likely land on the same answer.

hidden: Export reuses the delimiter inferred from the source
why: Nothing in the export section mentions the delimiter, and csv.writer's default comma is what a reference would emit.

hidden: A restarted instance answers without re-downloading
why: Can return the cached id is permissive, so a test cannot demand a hit, and a persisted-cache test would be phrased under STORAGE_DIR instead.

hidden: Only the effective value is parsed, so a garbage file entry masked by an env var starts fine
why: Most implementations merge raw strings before parsing, but a test pairing a bad file value with an env override is an unlikely fixture.

hidden: Filter validation runs first, so an unknown id with a bad filter is 400.
why: If id unknown return 404 is unconditional and every framework resolves the dataset before reading its columns.

hidden: Floats exported with a trailing .0 or strings JSON-quoted.
why: Semantically-correct CSV plus a required round trip pins values not bytes, so a divergent test would have to parse and still disagree.

hidden: Upload of bytes B and convert of a URL serving B share one id.
why: The two id rules key on different inputs and the tester asserts neither equality nor inequality, so only an equality test could bite.

hidden: An empty ORIGIN_ALLOWLIST value is an active allowlist that matches nothing.
why: No allowlist means all requests pass covers the empty case, and a test setting the variable to nothing is unlikely.
`hide` is the only valid value and no shape-dependent error is listed, so a 400 here would need an invented rule.
Tests that count origin hits under caching agree with the mandatory reading; the permissive reading would leave nothing to test.
Domain-boundary points squarely at label matching, and allowing the bare suffix is what any allowlist author would expect.
The one label the spec fixes is the lower-case family name, and "csv" is the only spelling that mirrors it.

hidden: Duplicate key is an invalid config file and the process exits
why: Last-wins is the convention and the likely dict-based reference behaviour; a strict reference is possible but less common.
file size and MAX_SOURCE_SIZE both name the document bytes; counting multipart framing would make the limit filename-dependent.
The unknown-id sentence is unconditional and lookup-before-validate is the default control flow, so a divergent 400 would need an unusual reference.

hidden: Unknown routes still 404 without a Referer
why: Before routing is explicit, so a per-route-decorator reference would contradict the text but few tests would probe the unknown-route case without a Referer.
Datasets must survive is the natural strong reading and the tester takes it, leaving little for a test to contradict.
The enrichment section explicitly leaves rows and total unchanged, and a blank-row spreadsheet fixture is an unlikely test choice.

hidden: Id derived from the full query string including charset.
why: Both the convert section and Determinism name only the source URL, so a test author hashing more than that would be ignoring two sentences.
`<dataset-id>` has one definition, the path segment, and a test would derive the filename from the endpoint it got back.
`force` is defined under the ingestion bypass and the query endpoint's control list is exhaustive, so a 400 test here is improbable.
Spec never constrains the id and a test that parsed its shape would have no sentence to point at, so tests almost surely only fetch the endpoint.
Writing the header for an empty result is what csv.writer does and what "export columns follow source column order" implies.
SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE, the settings table default true, and "fail startup" all point at an environment variable with a true default.
Steps 1-4 end in "Otherwise 403" and both allowlist error rows are 403, leaving nothing else for an unparseable Referer.

hidden: Empty DATAGATE_CONFIG is a read failure and the process exits
why: read failure at startup ... exits could cover an empty path, but a reference checking truthiness of the variable behaves as the tester chose.
upgrades stored state and "persisted datasets must survive restart" make persistence the only coherent reading.
Reading (2) is strictly stronger than (1), so no test of id stability can contradict it; only a fixed id format could, and nothing in the text hints at one.
Every listed reading leaves the same values as text, and no numeric-looking temporal form exists for a test to split them on.
First worksheet plus the must-be-tabular rule points at index 0, and a test would need to deliberately craft active or hidden sheets to disagree.
All other states keep enrichment off settles both the error question and case sensitivity.
Applies only on /convert plus the ignore rule for plain params leaves inertness as the only reading without an invented error.

hidden: Duplicate file parts are rejected as malformed multipart.
why: Two parts with the same name is an exotic fixture and every multipart parser hands back the first one.

hidden: Cache and fresh responses must share headers too.
why: The spec's contract is the JSON envelope and status everywhere else, and byte-identical headers are unsatisfiable, so tests compare bodies.

hidden: CACHE_ENABLED=false makes every upload replace stored data.
why: Every sentence of the cache section names /convert, and either reading yields the same upload id anyway.

hidden: An unusable STORAGE_DIR falls back to the default directory.
why: Create STORAGE_DIR if missing plus invalid config exits leaves little room for silently serving from another directory.

hidden: Enriched and plain ingestions of one source get different ids.
why: Upgrades stored state and the Determinism rule both require the same id, so a separate id would contradict two sentences.
Checkpoint 1 lists no parameter and later checkpoints add `_size`, so a test demanding an override at this stage is unlikely.
Every alternative yields the same status and envelope, so tests cannot distinguish them.
`enrich=yes` is introduced as an unconditional /convert option, and any first-time enrichment test would confirm the tester's reading.
Comparators are spelled lower-case, other name matching is stated case-sensitive, and an uppercase comparator is unlikely to be exercised at all.
Names are quoted in code style and multipart field names are conventionally exact; a mixed-case test is unlikely.
Tests must reach the server over plain HTTP to observe the absolute https endpoint, so refusing plaintext would defeat the tests themselves.
Replaces has no merge reading a test author would adopt.
Keyed by column name reads as a full mapping and a partial one has no textual support.

hidden: Query or export responses larger than the limit are refused.
why: Enforced for /convert and /upload names the routes explicitly and the accepted-at-limit rule would be pointless otherwise.

hidden: /convert with enrich=yes also returns the metadata.
why: Success response remains is restated verbatim right after the feature, which only makes sense if the convert reply does not grow.

hidden: force with enrich=yes is rejected or enrich is dropped.
why: Force forces re-ingestion and re-ingestion recomputes metadata compose without exception, and nothing rejects parameter combinations on /convert.
If /convert receives charset, use it is unconditional; no reading lets the origin header win.
The route is the dataset route plus a suffix and the unknown-id 404 rule is the only rule on offer.
replaces the cached dataset presupposes the same id and the determinism section says id is a function of source alone.
spreadsheet datasets is the class name and "excel" is what both containers share.
Headerless "CSV" is not a reading anyone writing an export test would take.
No error condition exists in any table for this case and the download happens either way.
The type column says bytes and no test author would count characters against it.
The error envelope is given verbatim as two keys, and "Responses include total" sits in the success description.
No parameter anywhere is case-insensitive and a test spelling FORCE is improbable.
No test is likely to place exotic whitespace around a boolean value; ASCII trim satisfies any plausible assertion.
